title: Design a Deck of Cards and Blackjack (OOD)
oneLiner: A reusable deck, then Blackjack on top of it: scoring aces, the dealer's rule, a round of play, and splits as the follow-up.
keyTakeaway: Keep the generic parts (card, deck, hand) free of any one game's rules and put Blackjack scoring in its own class. Count aces as 1 and add 10 once if it fits, shuffle with Fisher-Yates and an injected Random, and model a player's hands as a list so splitting doesn't need a redesign.
explanation:
Same format as the other OOD walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare and tick what you covered. The parking lot walk-through explains what an OOD round grades.

What's specific to the card game. It's a two-part question on purpose: first a generic deck, then a game that uses it. The interviewer is checking whether the generic part stays generic. A Card with a BlackjackValue property, or a Deck that knows about dealers, fails that test, because the same deck should work for poker. The small classes make it a good place to show judgement about inheritance: Player and Dealer extending a shared Participant is fine (one level, a real difference in behaviour), while HumanPlayer and BotPlayer subclasses are better as a decision policy the player holds.

The code is short, so it's expected to be right. Ace scoring is where most candidates slip (only one ace can ever count as 11), shuffling is where people reach for a biased shortcut, and settling a hand has an order that matters (a player who busts loses even if the dealer busts too). The classic follow-up is splitting pairs, which a design with one hand per player can't take without changes.
